universe: everything that exists
Sun: the star that Earth circles
planet: a large world that circles a star
gravity: the invisible pull that holds planets in orbit
star: a huge ball of burning gas that gives off light
galaxy: a vast group of billions of stars
Solar System: the Sun and everything that circles it

Tonight, when it is dark, go outside and look up. Those points of light are not small and they are not near. Each one is a burning sun, so far away that its light has been travelling towards your eyes for years, sometimes thousands of years. When you look at the stars, you are looking into the deep past.

image.note: A child lying on a mat at night looking up at a sky thick with stars; awe, quiet

pages.text: Everything you can see up there, and a great deal you cannot, is part of the universe. The universe is everything that exists: every star, every planet, every speck of dust, and all the empty space between. It is the biggest thing there is, because it is quite simply everything.

image.note: A widening view: rooftop, to Earth, to Sun and planets, to a galaxy, to many galaxies

pages.text: Let us start close to home. The Sun is not special to look at among the stars, but it is special to us, because it is ours. It is a giant ball of burning gas so large that more than a million Earths could fit inside it. Every scrap of warmth and light you have ever felt came from it.

image.note: The Sun beside a tiny Earth for scale; the size difference is the point

pages.text: The Sun is far too hot to touch or visit; near its surface, metal would boil away. Yet it sits at just the right distance from us. Any closer and the seas would boil. Any farther and they would freeze. We live on a world in exactly the right place, warmed by a fire ninety-three million miles away.

image.note: Earth glowing gently in the Sun's light, oceans and clouds visible; the "just right" distance shown

pages.text: The Sun does not travel alone. Eight planets circle it, held by an invisible pull called gravity, like children swinging round on the end of a rope. Together they make up the Solar System. Earth is the third planet out, a blue and white marble, the only world we know of that holds life.

image.note: The Solar System laid out, eight planets in orbit round the Sun; Earth marked

pages.text: The planets are wildly different. Mercury is a scorched rock. Venus is wrapped in poison cloud. Mars is a cold red desert where our machines now roam. Then come the giants: Jupiter, so huge all the other planets could fit inside it, and Saturn, wearing its beautiful rings of ice.

image.note: A line-up of the planets showing their true colours and relative sizes; Saturn's rings prominent

pages.text: Far out in the cold dark spin the ice worlds Uranus and Neptune, so distant that the Sun looks like just another bright star from there. Beyond them lie comets and lumps of rock, the leftovers from when the whole system was born. Our neighbourhood is stranger and larger than most people ever imagine.

image.note: The outer planets in deep blue darkness, the Sun a distant bright dot; lonely, vast

pages.text: So what exactly is a star? A star is an enormous ball of gas, so heavy that its own weight crushes its centre until it catches fire in a way no earthly fire ever could. That fire pours out light and heat for billions of years. Our Sun is a star. So is every point of light in the night sky.

image.note: A cutaway of a star showing its blazing core; simple, clear, dramatic

pages.text: Stars are not all the same. Some are small and cool and red. Some are huge and blazing blue. Stars are born inside great clouds of gas and dust, they shine for ages, and in the end they die, some quietly, some in a mighty explosion. Even stars have a beginning and an end.

image.note: A star nursery: a glowing cloud of gas with new stars lighting up inside it; colourful

pages.text: Now step back further. Our Sun is not alone. It belongs to a vast, slowly turning wheel of hundreds of billions of stars, called a galaxy. Ours is named the Milky Way. On a very dark night, far from city lights, you can actually see it: a pale band of light stretching across the whole sky.

image.note: The Milky Way arching over a dark African landscape; a child pointing up at it

pages.text: And here is the thought that stops the breath. The Milky Way is only one galaxy. Beyond it float billions more, each one packed with billions of stars of its own, scattered through space in every direction as far as any telescope can see. The universe is not big. Big is far too small a word.

image.note: A deep-space telescope image: countless galaxies filling the whole frame; overwhelming

pages.text: How can we hope to measure such a thing? By using light. Light is the fastest thing there is, yet even light takes time to cross space. The light reaching your eyes from a distant galaxy set off before there were any people at all. To look far into space is to look far back in time.

image.note: A beam of light travelling from a distant galaxy across ages to a child's eye; a timeline built of light

pages.text: Scientists have worked out that the whole universe began about fourteen thousand million years ago, in a single event, and that it has been growing ever since. Everything that exists, including the stuff that makes up you, was once part of that beginning. In a real way, you are made of ancient star.

image.note: A gentle image of a child's hand made of faint stardust, glowing from within; poetic, warm

pages.text: It would be easy to feel tiny. One person, on one planet, circling one ordinary star, in one galaxy among billions. And you are tiny. But hold on to this. In all that endless space, on all those countless worlds, you are, as far as anyone has ever found, part of the only place that can look up and wonder.

image.note: A single lit window in a dark estate, a child at it gazing up at the huge starry sky; small but glowing

pages.text: That is the strangest and finest thing of all. The universe made stars, and planets, and at least one small blue world where matter woke up and began to ask questions about itself. Every time you look up and wonder what is out there, the universe is, through you, wondering about itself.

image.note: The same child now smiling, the stars reflected in their eyes; connection, awe, closing
